title: Michael Y. Li (@michaelyli_) — thread (10 tweets)
summary:
[1/10] Can a language model learn, end-to-end, what to keep in its own KV cache and what to throw away? Can it learn to forget while it learns to reason?
Deep learning's central lesson: capability emerges from end-to-end optimization, not heuristics/strong inductive biases. But for efficiency, we rely heavily on hand-designed approaches.
🗑️ Introducing Neural Garbage Collection (NGC): we train a language model to jointly reason and manage its own KV cache, using reinforcement learning with outcome-based task reward alone. No SFT, no proxy objectives, no summarization in natural language.
New paper with @jubayer_hamid, Emily Fox, and @noahdgoodman!
📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/HGh18slacAAyDNS.png
────────
[2/10] LMs are already trained to reason with RL, where every token is a discrete action sampled from the model and shaped by task reward. So it’s natural to cast KV cache eviction as another discrete action sampled from the same LM.
A single outcome-based task reward then jointly trains the LM to reason and manage its KV cache end-to-end: what the model evicts shapes what it remembers → what it remembers shapes its reasoning → the correctness of that reasoning is the reward. 3/n
📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/HGh2cmWaoAEZMO7.png
────────
[3/10] When LMs think longer, they can solve problems that are otherwise out of reach, but this rapidly grows the KV cache, creating a bottleneck to test-time scaling.
Our approach: let RL train the LM to both reason and manage its KV cache. Concretely, as the LM reasons, it periodically pauses, (1) scores its KV cache, (2) samples cache evictions, and (3) continues reasoning from the pruned cache. 2/n
────────
[4/10] The results: at 2-4× reduction in peak KV cache size, NGC significantly outperforms hand-designed baselines for cache management on AIME 2025 and Countdown and maintains strong reasoning performance relative to full-cache upper bound. 4/n
📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/HGh2m27b0AA5a2r.png
────────
[5/10] Second — make cache evictions efficiently sampleable. Cache eviction is typically deterministic. To leverage policy gradients, we make it a stochastic action with an exact log-probability by sampling cache evictions via the Gumbel top-k trick using the scores computed by the LM.
Both cache evictions and tokens are discrete actions with tractable log-probs. We can then use policy gradients, the workhorse behind training reasoning models, to train the LM to produce both cache evictions and reasoning tokens. 6/n
────────
[6/10] But how do we make this work?
First — a new kind of action. LMs produce tokens. They were never trained, during pre-training or SFT, to act on their own cache. So how do we ask one to?
We score cache entries with the LM’s own attention mechanism. Pre-training already gives it a good prior over what's relevant. No new parameters. No separate scoring module. No training beyond RLVR itself. 5/n
────────
[7/10] Third — policy gradients through a dynamically changing state. In standard RLVR, the state only grows: each token is sampled conditioned on everything before it. In NGC, this is no longer true: the model edits its own context mid-reasoning by evicting cache entries.
We account for this when training the LM using replay attention masks that reconstruct exactly what each token could see when it was sampled. One forward pass with these replay masks gives correct log-probs for every sampled token in parallel. 7/n
📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/HGh3BfWaEAAXMDS.png
────────
[8/10] Bonus: we can make the model aware of its own budget.
Before the LM reasons, we put the eviction rate in the prompt: <eviction_rate>50%</eviction_rate>. The model “senses” its memory constraint before it thinks.
We call this budget-aware interoception. It gives an 8–13% boost at aggressive compression rates and improves generalization to budgets the model wasn't trained on. 9/n
📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/HGh3wtoagAA0dmk.jpg
────────
[9/10] Put it together, and the recipe is simple: in addition to generating tokens, the LM periodically makes another kind of discrete decision (which cache entries to evict).
A single outcome-based reward trains everything. No SFT. No teacher model. No auxiliary objectives. No separate training stages.
End-to-end optimization pressure alone shapes how the model reasons and what it forgets. 8/n
────────
[10/10] This paper is a first step towards a broader vision we’re really excited by: the same end-to-end optimization that drives capability can also drive efficiency, enabling an additional dimension of self-improvement in which language models become more capable and more efficient.
Link to paper: 10/n

title: Michael Y. Li (@michaelyli_)
summary:
Excited to share our new work on training language models to use multiple axes of inference compute — sequential, parallel, and aggregative — end-to-end, led by @jubayer_hamid and @ifdita_hasan.
LLMs already use many forms of compute at test time, so they should learn to use them during training too.
How do we train this? Learning to synthesize a better answer from multiple attempts can be handled with standard RL. The harder problem is teaching models to generate a set of traces that are useful together for a downstream synthesizer to produce a better final response. This leads naturally to a set RL formulation for training models to generate these traces.
Quoting @jubayer_hamid
The most capable reasoning systems in AI scale inference compute along several axes: sequential compute to think longer, parallel compute to sample many independent attempts, and aggregative compute to synthesize prior traces into a new improved one. But during training, we only optimize how models use sequential compute. This creates a fundamental mismatch between how we ultimately deploy these systems and how we train them, leaving much of search and synthesis unoptimized.
We introduce SPIRAL, an RL framework for making all inference-compute primitives end-to-end learnable: models learn to coordinate sequential, parallel, and aggregative reasoning using only the reward of the final output. Work with @ifdita_hasan (co-lead), @michaelyli_ , @oshaikh13 , @yoonholeee , @DorsaSadigh , @chelseabfinn , @noahdgoodman 🧵
📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/HLg6ke0bYAA-B71.jpg

title: Michael Y. Li (@michaelyli_) — thread (11 tweets)
summary:
[1/11] You're wasting FLOPs when scaling inference compute: by independently sampling parallel attempts, you burn compute rediscovering the same solutions.
Introducing QuasiMoTTo: we scale parallel sampling with correlated samples instead! These samples have higher coverage, are marginally exact draws from the LLM, and can be generated in parallel.
Result: same performance with 25-47% fewer samples in test-time scaling + 50% fewer training steps in RL!
In our new paper, we explore the design space of correlated samplers. Work with co-authors @probablynotaz9 (co-lead), @gandhikanishk, @noahdgoodman, and Emily Fox!
📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/HMPSgxgaMAADiR-.jpg
────────
[2/11] RL results. In GRPO, by swapping out the i.i.d. sampler for a correlated sampler, we see sample efficiency improvements: same reward in fewer training steps.
Where do the gains come from? The increase in coverage reduces the percentage of zero-variance groups, boosting the effective batch size.
With i.i.d. sampling, rollouts in a group frequently coincide, so the group-relative advantage collapses to zero, providing no gradient signal.
3/n
📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/HMPUp7SbkAA6F-F.jpg
────────
[3/11] Test-time scaling results. QuasiMoTTo samples have higher coverage, achieving higher pass@k than i.i.d. sampling for the same budget k.
QuasiMoTTo even saturates a theoretical upper bound for any marginal-preserving sampler!
2/n
📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/HMPVZZUagAEd7xD.jpg
────────
[4/11] Trick 1: inverse-CDF sampling + arithmetic coding
How to sample one discrete variable? Split [0,1] into bins with widths = probs, sample uniformly, see which bin you land in. For sequences? Same trick but use arithmetic coding, which maps every sequence to a subinterval of [0,1] whose length = probability of sequence under LLM.
In more detail: sample a uniform u. Split [0,1] into bins with sizes equal to first-token probabilities p(x_1). Step into the bin containing u and "collect" that token. Now repeat inside that bin with p(x_2|x_1), and so on…
Since a uniform u lands in a sequence's subinterval with probability = interval length = sequence probability, this procedure yields exact samples.
5/n
📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/HMPTQWgacAAXjOH.jpg
────────
[5/11] But how do you correlate samples from an LLM?
Two tricks:
(1) Arithmetic coding + inverse-CDF sampling. N uniform points on [0,1] -> N rollouts.
(2) Quasi-Monte Carlo (QMC) chooses those N points to be more evenly spread than i.i.d., but each point is uniform (marginally).
This arithmetic sampling approach was introduced in Vilnis et al. 2022 (arXiv:2210.15458) and for a review of arithmetic coding see David MacKay’s wonderful book.
4/n
────────
[6/11] Sampling is embarrassingly parallel. Intuitively, the LLM arithmetic code defines a trie. Given its own uniform u_i, each rollout i is a separate traversal of the same trie; there is no communication between rollouts. All coordination happens upfront from the N coupled uniforms.
7/n
────────
[7/11] Trick 2: high-coverage batch via randomized QMC.
We want samples spread apart, but each sample must be marginally uniform for inverse-CDF to be correct. How to do this? Toy example: sample u~Unif[0,1] and consider (u, 1−u). Each coordinate is uniform, but samples never collide.
We use randomized QMC to generate N uniform samples.
The lattice construction is intuitive. Generate points on the unit circle with fixed spacing and then rotate all points by the same randomly sampled angle. Rotation preserves relative distances, but makes each individual point marginally uniform, so pushing them through the inverse CDF yields correctly distributed samples.
6/n
📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/HMPTZk_bEAAP8Rr.jpg
────────
[8/11] How does the choice of QMC sampler impact the results? Intuitively, there's a freedom vs. coverage tradeoff:
i.i.d. -> total freedom, weak coverage
stratified -> points repel (can’t land in the same stratum), better coverage
lattice -> one point determines all others, max coverage
9/n
📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/HMPUY_caUAAyDZD.jpg
────────
[9/11] The standard pass@k estimator assumes independent samples! We develop an analogous unbiased bootstrap estimator for QMC.
To estimate pass@k given N > k samples, we first construct a fine grid of N points, then subsample k < N points by skipping with an appropriate stride.
8/n
📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/HMPUPJ1a0AAKFGc.png
────────
[10/11] This project started as a nerd snipe: we joked about reviving an older paper on antithetic sampling ( Then we were reminded of the inverse-CDF trick while playing with vLLM — and then I randomly walked past Art Owen!
Also, shout-out to my awesome co-lead on this project (a co-term!) Anthony Zhan @probablynotaz9!!
Lastly, we build on these great papers: arithmetic sampling (arXiv:2210.15458) and CARMS (arXiv:2110.14002).
11/n
────────
[11/11] This paper applies ideas from the Monte Carlo literature to scaling inference compute and RL (shout-out to Art Owen and others!). This is a rich design space that we’re excited by!
Paper:
10/n

title: Michael Y. Li (@michaelyli_) — thread (10 tweets)
clean_title: Self-play pretraining with zero data generates useful learning structure
summary:
[1/10] Can an LM, starting from random init (!!), learn to generate all of its pretraining data?
Introducing Self-Play Pretraining with Zero Data. Two models start from random initialization: a generator proposes programs for a universal Turing machine and a learner trains on their outputs. We never train on any real data, but see predictable scaling on natural datasets: zero-shot val loss on images, text, audio, and melodies decreases predictably with self-play compute. And the learner develops in-context learning capabilities.
A fun proof-of-concept, co-led with @AdityaCowsik and @KfirDolev and co-authors @gbruno_dl, @ANourya @noahdgoodman, and @YoavLevine.
📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/HTE9rwmb0AAECYJ.jpg
────────
[2/10] What is the intuition behind this method and why self-play?
Solomonoff induction characterizes an idealized, uncomputable next-token predictor: assuming only that the data are generated by some computable process, it predicts by considering every program that could have generated the data, with a preference for shorter programs. This simplicity bias favors regularities that admit short descriptions, such as repetition, reuse, and composition, and such structure can recur across otherwise very different modalities. By running programs on a universal Turing machine, we get a broad space of synthetic data that can, in principle, represent any computable data-generating process and contains such regularities.
But this space is enormous, and which programs are useful depends on what the learner already knows. We therefore use self-play to adaptively search this space for data that is useful to the current learner. Because the space contains structure shared across many data-generating processes, learning on this synthetic data can transfer to natural data.
Together, self-play and a universal space of programs yield a general method that leverages compute, in the spirit of the Bitter Lesson.
2/n
────────
[3/10] Self-play scales predictably across modalities and adaptivity to the learner matters.
To isolate the value of adaptivity, we compare against a fixed universal prior over programs: the same universal search space, but without adapting to the learner. It scales much more slowly.
We also compare against PCFG pretraining, finding that it scales well on text and code but less consistently across non-language modalities.
4/n
📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/HTE-XuDbIAAdMrg.jpg
────────
[4/10] How do we train the learner and the generator?
The learner is trained via standard next-token prediction on output bytes from the programs generated by the generator. But what about the generator? We train it with RL.
A simple difficulty-based reward fails: a program can make its output arbitrarily hard to predict by injecting random bytes, without introducing useful structure.
We want to match programs to the frontier of what the learner can actually learn. We therefore reward programs whose gradients have large overlap with the learner’s recent learning trajectory, measured by the magnitude of the AdamW-preconditioned inner product between the gradient on a program’s output and the learner’s recent parameter movement.
3/n
────────
[5/10] The generator improves during self-play.
Later generator checkpoints produce more useful training data: fresh learners trained from scratch on their samples transfer better to natural datasets.
6/n
📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/HTE-rIpbEAAZKfm.jpg
────────
[6/10] Self-play gives rise to in-context learning.
With more ICL examples, the model trained with self-play improves across all six tasks; fixed universal-prior pretraining largely fails, while PCFG pretraining transfers mainly to associative recall.
5/n
📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/HTFBFyPbsAA68Rz.jpg
────────
[7/10] Links!
9/n
────────
[8/10] We explain our results with a simple ansatz.
Loosely, natural data mixes contingent information (facts about our world) with universal predictive structure (composition, repetition, recursion, etc…) that are not specific to our world. Our self-play approach only supplies the latter. However, if it produces universal structure efficiently, and if universal structure is the bottleneck, predictable scaling on natural data follows. We make this more precise in the paper.
8/n
────────
[9/10] Interesting mathematical structure emerges from self-play more quickly than random sampling.
The generator discovers programs that generate outputs with interesting structure that would take a long time to sample under the universal prior.
7/n
📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/HTE-yifbEAAULT4.png
────────
[10/10] On a personal note, this was a fun collaboration at the intersection of things we’ve been excited by for a while: self-play, Solomonoff induction, universal prediction. This is an initial step and we think there are a lot of exciting directions worth exploring!
Among many others, we were inspired by these papers on universal prediction, Solomonoff induction, self-play, and pretraining under infinite compute: arXiv:2401.14953, arXiv:2509.14786, arXiv:2506.20057, arXiv:2407.00695, and arXiv:2604.20209.
And of course Solomonoff ’64
10/n
clean_summary:
Usually, language models learn from huge datasets of real text, images, or audio. But Michael Y. Li and collaborators ask: can a model start from scratch and learn useful patterns without any real data? They propose self-play pretraining, where two models start randomly—one generates programs for a universal Turing machine, and the other learns from their outputs. This synthetic data contains broad computable structures that appear across many modalities.

The generator improves by rewarding programs that help the learner make progress, measured by gradient alignment. This adaptive self-play scales predictably and leads the learner to develop in-context learning abilities. Compared to fixed program distributions or PCFG pretraining, self-play better transfers to natural data. The team sees this as a step toward universal prediction, inspired by Solomonoff induction, where learning focuses on discovering universal, reusable structure rather than specific facts.

title: Michael Y. Li (@michaelyli_)
summary:
Trust the Critic More
"We introduce Actor-Critic with Action Chunking (AC2) that removes the need to roll every trajectory to completion. AC2 instead assigns credit to action chunks: short continuations of prefixes of past trajectories. A learned critic scores the state reached at the end of each action chunk, allowing the policy to update without observing a terminal reward."
"First, we introduce local readiness which uses critic-based updates on a problem only when the critic is sufficiently accurate on that particular problem. Second, when available, we provide the critic with a reference solution from a previous successful rollout. Third, we assign credit over action chunks of 10k tokens rather than individual tokens, giving the critic a more meaningful portion of the trajectory to evaluate."
Link:

summary:
Great researchers have an uncanny ability to make connections that seem inevitable in hindsight, in places nobody else would have thought to look. Can we measure this ability?
Introducing ScholarCatalyst: a far-from-saturated benchmark for finding what we call "catalyst papers"📚, labeled by 184 lead authors on 207 of their own recent projects.
Paper:
To make sustained progress on open-ended problems, I think agents need the sort of "research taste" that great researchers have. They need to make deep connections between earlier discoveries and problems those discoveries weren't intended to solve. ScholarCatalyst is a first step towards this goal.
More details in the thread below🧵

title: Michael Y. Li (@michaelyli_)
clean_title: Actor-Critic with Action Chunking speeds up RL training for LLMs
summary:
Do you really need to finish every rollout in RL for LLM? Not if you make your critic better—and trust it!
We propose Actor-Critic with Action Chunking (AC2): use a learned critic to score chunks of tokens => only need partial rollouts ⇒ train faster than GRPO!
📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/HTozGDfbUAAefT8.jpg
clean_summary:
In reinforcement learning (RL) for large language models (LLMs), you usually finish every rollout to evaluate actions, which can be slow. Michael Y. Li suggests you don't need to complete every rollout if you improve your critic—a model that estimates how good partial answers are—and trust its scores.

He proposes Actor-Critic with Action Chunking (AC2), which scores chunks of tokens instead of full sequences. This means you only need partial rollouts, allowing training to proceed faster than methods like GRPO.

title: Michael Y. Li (@michaelyli_)
clean_title: Switching Linear Attention balances expressiveness and fixed state size
summary:
Softmax attention is expressive, but its KV cache grows with sequence length. Linear attention keeps a fixed state size, but is less expressive.
In our #COLM2026 paper, Switching Linear Attention (SwiLA) gets the best of both worlds by switching among multiple linear maps 🧵
📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/HT4WLUabEAARvEZ.jpg
clean_summary:
Softmax attention is powerful because it can express complex relationships, but its key-value (KV) cache grows as the sequence gets longer, which can be costly. Linear attention keeps the state size fixed regardless of sequence length, saving memory, but it is less expressive.

Michael Y. Li presents Switching Linear Attention (SwiLA) in his COLM 2026 paper. SwiLA switches among multiple linear maps, aiming to combine the expressiveness of softmax attention with the fixed state size advantage of linear attention.

title: Michael Y. Li (@michaelyli_)
clean_title: Priced Guidance measures LLMs' ability to generate novel research ideas
summary:
Can LLMs generate novel research ideas? We propose Priced Guidance to quantify this via compression!
We lower bound P(LLM forecasts a future paper’s idea X). Instead of sampling ideas until X is matched, the LLM plays “20 Questions” to recover X, charging each hint by surprisal.
📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/HT8Ae71bgAAVUl6.jpg
clean_summary:
You might wonder if large language models (LLMs) can come up with truly new research ideas. Michael Y. Li proposes Priced Guidance, a way to measure this by treating idea generation like a compression problem.

Instead of randomly guessing ideas until the model hits the target, the LLM plays a “20 Questions” game to reconstruct the idea, paying a cost for each hint based on how surprising it is. This approach gives a lower bound on the probability that the LLM can predict a future paper’s idea, quantifying its creativity more efficiently.
